nameStory: The Common Redshank gets its straightforward name from its most obvious feature - those bright reddish-orange legs that seem to glow against muddy shorelines. The word 'shank' refers to the lower leg portion, and this bird's vibrant red shanks make it instantly recognizable among the often confusing world of brown shorebirds.
description: The Common Redshank is a medium-sized shorebird about the size of a robin, with a sleek brown body streaked with darker markings. Its most striking features are its bright red-orange legs and matching red base to its straight, pointed bill. This Eurasian visitor belongs to the sandpiper family but is an extremely rare sight in New England, with only one confirmed observation in the region. It has a graceful, alert posture and moves with quick, darting steps along shorelines.

idTips.label: Bright red-orange legs
idTips.description: The legs are a vivid reddish-orange color that stands out dramatically against muddy or sandy backgrounds, much brighter than the yellowish legs of yellowlegs

idTips.label: Red-based bill
idTips.description: The straight bill has a bright red or orange base that matches the legs, with the tip being dark - this two-toned bill is distinctive

idTips.label: Brown streaked plumage
idTips.description: The body appears warm brown with darker streaking, giving it a mottled appearance that helps it blend with mudflats and shoreline debris

idTips.label: White wing patches in flight
idTips.description: When it takes off, watch for distinctive white patches on the wings and white on the rump that flash conspicuously against the brown body

idTips.label: Alert, upright posture
idTips.description: Stands more upright than many sandpipers, often bobbing its head and appearing nervous or watchful, ready to take flight at the first sign of danger

habitat: If you're incredibly lucky to spot one, look along mudflats, salt marshes, and shallow coastal pools where other shorebirds gather. They prefer areas with soft mud where they can probe for worms and small crustaceans. In their native range, they also use freshwater marshes and wet meadows, but any New England sighting would most likely be along the coast during migration.

seasonality.spring: The most likely time to encounter this rarity in New England, as occasional vagrants may appear during spring migration from late April through May among flocks of other shorebirds.
seasonality.summer: Extremely unlikely to be seen, as they would be on breeding grounds in Europe and Asia during this time.
seasonality.fall: Another possible but very rare migration window from August through September, when young birds might occasionally wander off course during their first migration.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters, as they typically winter in warmer climates of Africa and southern Asia.

funFact: Common Redshanks are so wary and quick to sound alarm calls that other shorebirds have learned to trust their warnings - they're essentially the neighborhood watch birds of European mudflats, alerting entire flocks to approaching danger with their loud, piercing calls.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Lesser or Greater Yellowlegs, but remember 'red legs, red legs!' as your memory trick - no other similar-sized shorebird in New England has those bright orange-red legs. The yellowlegs have (obviously) yellow legs, and Willets have grayish legs.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of those 'mega-rare' birds that sends birders scrambling when one shows up - with only one confirmed New England record, spotting a Common Redshank here would be the find of a lifetime and likely make regional birding news.
compareHints: Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build. Unlike the yellowlegs with their thin yellow legs and bills, the Redshank's orange-red legs and red-based bill make it unmistakable. It's also chunkier and more compact than the elegant, long-legged yellowlegs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either.
Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely.
Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones.
Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species.
